summary: Defines common semantics and data formats for presence so gateways can connect different presence services. When it was written, many instant messaging systems used incompatible protocols, with little interoperability between them.

plainLanguage.summary: Presence is the practice of telling others whether you are available, busy or away. CPP describes that exchange in a protocol-neutral way: an application asks to watch someone's presence, the service answers, and it sends a notification whenever the answer changes. A gateway can then use this common description to connect two different presence systems.

questions: presence interoperability between instant messaging services
what is the common profile for presence
what is the pres uri scheme
how do you unsubscribe from presence
subtitle: A shared abstract model of presence so gateways can link instant messaging services that speak different protocols.

tldr.problem: Many presence protocols, mostly parts of commercial instant messaging services, were in use, and little interoperability between them had been achieved.
tldr.mechanism: CPP defines three abstract operations (subscribe, response and notify), a pres: URI scheme and a requirement to carry presence in the PIDF format, so that gateways can map between services.
tldr.outcome: A presence protocol that supports all of the operations can connect to a CPP gateway. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no replacement.

facts.label: TransID and SubscriptID length
facts.value: Gateways should handle up to 40 bytes

today: RFC 3859 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2004. The metadata for this unit records no later RFC that obsoletes or updating it. The RFC builds on the presence model of RFC 2778 and the security requirements of RFC 2779, and it registers the pres URI scheme with IANA.

sections.title: Why a Common Profile
sections.content:
Presence is defined in RFC 2778. At the time this document was written, numerous presence protocols were in use, largely as components of commercial instant messaging services, and little interoperability between services based on these protocols had been achieved. This specification defines semantics and data formats for common services of presence, to facilitate the creation of gateways between presence services: a common profile for presence, or CPP.

Service behavior is described abstractly, in terms of operations invoked between the consumer and the provider of a service. Each presence service must specify how that behavior is mapped onto its own protocol interactions, and the choice of strategy is a local matter as long as the relation between the abstract behavior and the protocol is clear. One strategy might transmit presence information as key/value pairs, another might use a compact binary representation, and a third might use nested containers. The parameters for each operation are defined using an abstract syntax, which fixes the range of possible data values, and each presence service must specify how well-formed instances of that representation are encoded as a concrete series of bits.

To give end-to-end features, especially security, a way to pass through presence interoperability gateways, the specification also recommends presence document formats that presence protocols could use.
sections.plainLanguage: Different presence systems used different protocols, so a program on one could not talk to a program on the other. CPP gives them a shared vocabulary: the same few operations, the same way to name people, and the same way to write presence information, so a gateway can translate between them.

sections.title: The Vocabulary
sections.content:
The memo uses the vocabulary of RFC 2778, so terms such as CLOSED, INSTANT INBOX, PRESENCE and OPEN carry the meanings given there. It adds two terms of its own.

The term gateway denotes a network element responsible for interworking between diverse presence protocols. Although the presence protocols are diverse, under the model in this document they can carry a common payload relayed by the gateway. Whether these interworking intermediaries should be called gateways or relays is therefore debatable, and the document calls them CPP gateways.

The term presence service derives from RFC 2778, but its meaning shifts slightly because of the gateways. When a client sends an operation to a presence service, that service might be an endpoint or an intermediary such as a CPP gateway, and the client should not have to know which it is addressing, because responses from either appear the same.

For a compliant protocol to interface with a presence gateway it must support all of the operations described in the document, meaning it must have some message or capability that provides the function of every given operation. The attributes defined for the operations must likewise correspond to information available in the protocol. Those attributes are the minimum needed for interoperability: the functions in a presence protocol that correspond to these operations may carry additional information that CPP will not map.
sections.plainLanguage: The document borrows its terms from the earlier presence model and adds one: a gateway, the box that sits between two presence systems and translates for them.

sections.title: Subscribe, Response and Notify
sections.content:
When an application wants to subscribe to the presence information associated with a PRESENTITY, in order to receive periodic notifications of that information, it invokes the subscribe operation. The operation has the attributes watcher, target, duration, SubscriptID and TransID. The watcher and target identify the WATCHER and the PRESENTITY. The duration is the maximum number of seconds the subscription should be active, and may be zero, which makes it a one-time request for presence information. The SubscriptID creates a reference to the subscription that is used when unsubscribing. The TransID is a unique identifier used to correlate the subscribe operation with its response, and gateways should be capable of handling TransIDs and SubscriptIDs up to 40 bytes in length.

On receiving a subscribe operation the service immediately responds by invoking the response operation with the same TransID. The response carries status, TransID and duration. The status says whether the subscribe operation succeeded or failed, the TransID matches the operation being answered, and the duration gives the number of seconds for which the subscription will be active, which may differ from the value requested.

If the response indicates success, the service immediately invokes the notify operation to communicate the presence information to the watcher. Notify carries the attributes watcher, target and TransID, where the watcher and target values are identical to those of the subscribe operation that triggered it and the TransID is unique to that notification. Notify also carries content, the presence information itself.

If the duration parameter is non-zero, then for up to the specified duration the service invokes notify whenever there are changes to the presentity's presence information. Otherwise exactly one notify is invoked, achieving a one-time poll. There is no application response to notify in CPP.
sections.plainLanguage: Three operations do all the work. An application subscribes, the service answers immediately, and the service then sends a notification whenever the person's status changes. The subscription may have a time limit, and a duration of zero means just ask once.

sections.title: Naming Presentities and Watchers
sections.content:
A PRESENTITY is specified using the PRES URI scheme, described in Appendix A of the RFC, for example pres:fred@example.com. WATCHERs identify themselves in the same manner as presentities, that is, with a pres URI.

Address resolution follows from that naming. A presence service client determines the next hop to forward an operation to by resolving the domain name portion of the service destination, and compliant implementations SHOULD follow the guidelines for dereferencing URIs given in RFC 3861.

The IANA has assigned the pres URI scheme, which designates an Internet resource, namely a presentity or watcher. The syntax of a pres URI follows the existing mailto: URI syntax specified in RFC 2368.
sections.plainLanguage: People are named with an address of the form pres:name@example.com. The part after the at sign is a domain name, and the client looks that name up in DNS to work out where to send the operation.

sections.title: The Format of Presence Information
sections.content:
The specification defines an abstract interoperability mechanism for presence protocols, and the message content definition given in it pertains to semantics rather than syntax. However, some important properties for interoperability can only be provided if a common end-to-end format for presence is employed by the interoperating protocols, especially with respect to security. To maintain end-to-end security properties, applications that send notification operations through a CPP gateway MUST support the format defined in PIDF, RFC 3863. Applications MAY support other content formats.

CPP gateways MUST be capable of relaying the body of a notification operation between supported presence protocols without needing to modify or inspect the content. That is what makes end-to-end protection survive the trip through a gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: The text of a presence message has a agreed format, PIDF, so that a gateway can pass it along without reading it. Because the gateway never opens the message, any encryption or signature on it still holds on the other side.

sections.title: How the Service Processes a Subscribe
sections.content:
An implementation of the service must maintain information about presence information and continual operations, such as periodic notification, in persistent storage. The subscription identifier is potentially long-lived, so the values generated for it should be unique across a significant duration of time, and should be intrinsically globally unique over time rather than merely unique among operations sent to or from a particular watcher and presentity.

When the service is informed of a subscribe operation it performs these steps. If the watcher or target parameter does not refer to a valid presentity, it invokes a response operation with status failure. If access control does not permit the application to request the operation, it invokes a response with status failure. If the duration parameter is non-zero and the watcher and target parameters refer to an in-progress subscribe operation for the application, it invokes a response with status failure.

Otherwise, if the service is able to deliver the message, it immediately invokes a response operation with status success, conveying in it any different duration the service has chosen for the subscription, and then immediately invokes a notify operation with the target's presence information for the watcher. For up to the amount of time indicated by the duration parameter, measured from the time the subscribe operation was received, a notify operation is invoked for the watcher if the target's presence information changes and access control allows it. When the duration is zero the subscribe operation is a one-time poll, so the continued notifications do not occur. In every case the TransID in the response is identical to the one in the subscribe operation.

To terminate a subscription the application issues a subscribe with duration zero and the SubscriptID of the existing subscription. There is no independent unsubscribe operation, and to ask for presence information once without starting a subscription the application issues a subscribe with duration zero and a new SubscriptID; there is no independent fetch operation. A notify operation is invoked when a subscription is canceled in this fashion, and the watcher may discard it.
sections.plainLanguage: The service checks that the request is valid and allowed, then confirms it and sends the current status. It keeps sending updates until the subscription runs out. Cancelling and asking for a one-off status are the same request with a duration of zero, so there is no separate unsubscribe.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Detailed security considerations for presence protocols are given in RFC 2779. CPP defines an interoperability function used by gateways between presence protocols, and CPP gateways MUST be compliant with the minimum security requirements of the presence protocols with which they interface.

Introducing gateways into the security model of RFC 2779 also introduces new risks. End-to-end security properties, especially confidentiality and integrity, between presentities and watchers that interface through a CPP gateway can only be provided if a common presence format, such as the format described in RFC 3863, is supported by the protocols interfacing with the gateway.

When end-to-end security is required, the notify operation MUST use PIDF and MUST secure the PIDF MIME body with S/MIME, using encryption (CMS EnvelopeData) and/or S/MIME signatures (CMS SignedData). The S/MIME algorithms are set by CMS. AES should be preferred, since it is expected to suit the capabilities of many platforms; implementations MAY use AES as an encryption algorithm but are REQUIRED to support only the baseline algorithms mandated by S/MIME and CMS.

When PRES URIs are used in presence protocols they convey the identity of watchers and presentities. Certificates used for S/MIME presence operations SHOULD, for the purposes of reference integrity, contain a subjectAltName field holding the PRES URI of their subject. Users and service providers are encouraged to employ trust anchors for certificates that are widely accepted rather than trust anchors specific to one presence service or provider. Anonymous presence services are mentioned as something that may be desired in some cases, and are beyond the scope of this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Because a gateway sits in the middle, the message has to be protected end to end or the gateway can read or change it. The RFC therefore requires the standard presence format to be encrypted or signed with S/MIME when that level of protection is wanted.
